method: A metric modulation keeps one note value's real duration while changing the value it is written as, so the new quarter-note tempo is the old tempo x new note value / old note value. Note values are measured in quarter notes: whole 4, dotted half 3, half 2, dotted quarter 1.5, quarter 1, dotted eighth 0.75, eighth 0.5, dotted sixteenth 0.375, sixteenth 0.25, thirty-second 0.125, half-note triplet 4/3, quarter-note triplet 2/3 and eighth-note triplet 1/3. At 120 BPM the old dotted quarter lasts 750 ms; written as the new quarter it gives 120 x 1 / 1.5 = 80 BPM, and the new quarter also lasts 750 ms. The tempo ratio and the beat equivalence are reduced to whole numbers with the greatest common divisor. Tempo must be a number from 1 to 1,000 BPM and decimal commas are accepted; a missing tempo, a non-numeric tempo, an out-of-range tempo or an unknown note value is refused by name. Results are rounded to three decimals. This is notation timing, not a performance or groove model; everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Calcophony, How to Calculate Metric Modulation: Tempo Pivots Explained - newBPM = oldBPM x new pivot value / old pivot value, with the pivot keeping its real duration
Wikipedia, Metric modulation: a tempo change in which a note value from the old tempo becomes a different note value in the new tempo
Note values in quarter notes: dotted values multiply by 3/2, triplets by 2/3, and halving or doubling a value halves or doubles its length
